summary: Defines a generalized method of fragmentation for PWE3 protocols and services, so large pseudowire payloads can be split and rebuilt. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4623 says how a pseudowire frame that is too large for the network path can be split into pieces, sent across the tunnel, and put back together at the far end. Two bits in the frame header mark whether a piece is the first, the last or one in the middle, and a sequence number puts them in order. The RFC also says clearly that this should only be used when managing the maximum packet size has failed.

subtitle: How a pseudowire frame that is too big for the network is split up, marked and put back together.

tldr.problem: A pseudowire carries an emulated service across a packet network, and the payload plus its headers can be larger than the path MTU. When the frame cannot be split by the network itself, something has to break it up and put it back together.
tldr.mechanism: The sending provider edge router fragments the frame just before it encapsulates it, and the receiving router reassembles it just after it decapsulates it. Two bits, B and E, mark the first, last and middle fragments, a sequence number orders them, and the location of those bits is defined for the MPLS control word and for L2TPv2 and L2TPv3 headers.
tldr.outcome: The result is one fragmentation method that works across the pseudowire protocols, with signalling so a sender only fragments for a peer that has said it can reassemble. The RFC is explicit that fragmentation is a last resort, since it costs processing in the core of the network.

facts.label: MPLS control word bits
facts.value: B and E in positions 8 and 9

facts.label: L2TPv3 sublayer bits
facts.value: B and E in bits 2 and 3

facts.label: L2TPv2 header bits
facts.value: B and E in bits 8 and 9

today: RFC 4623 is a Proposed Standard from August 2006 and is neither obsoleted nor updated. It adds to the PWE3 architecture document RFC 3985, reuses the control word of RFC 4385 and the L2TPv3 and L2TPv2 headers, and asks IANA to register two L2TP attribute values and four reserved bits.

sections.title: Introduction and the Fragmentation Domain
sections.content:
The PWE3 architecture document defines a network reference model in which a customer edge router and a provider edge router sit on either side of an emulated service, and a pseudowire carries that service between the two provider edge routers across a packet switched network tunnel.

A pseudowire payload is normally relayed across the pseudowire as a single IP or MPLS packet switched network PDU. There are cases, however, where the combined size of the payload and its associated PWE3 and PSN headers exceeds the path MTU. When a packet exceeds the MTU of a given network, fragmentation and reassembly will let it traverse the network and reach its destination.

This document defines a generalized method of performing that fragmentation for use with all PWE3 protocols and services. It should be used only in cases where MTU management methods fail. Because of the increased processing overhead, fragmentation and reassembly in core network devices should always be considered something to avoid whenever possible.

The fragmentation and reassembly domain sits between the two provider edge routers. Fragmentation takes place in the transmitting router immediately before pseudowire encapsulation, and reassembly takes place in the receiving router immediately after pseudowire decapsulation. A sequence number is necessary for both procedures, so using the Sequence Number field on fragmented packets is required. The order of operation is that fragmentation is performed first, and the resulting fragments are then assigned sequential sequence numbers.

Depending on the encapsulation in use, the value 0 may not be part of the sequence number space, in which case its use for fragmentation must follow the same rule: as the sequence number is incremented it skips zero and wraps from 65535 to 1. If 0 is part of the space, then the same sequence space is used for fragmentation and reassembly.
sections.plainLanguage: The frame is split at the router that sends it into the tunnel, and put back together at the router that takes it out. Each piece is numbered so the receiver can order them, and the numbering follows whatever rule the tunnel already uses.

sections.title: Alternatives to PWE3 Fragmentation
sections.content:
Fragmentation and reassembly in network equipment generally needs significantly greater resources than sending a packet as a single unit, so it should be avoided whenever possible. The ideal solutions are proper configuration and management of MTU sizes between the customer edge router and the provider edge router and across the packet switched network, together with adaptive measures that operate with the originating host, such as path MTU discovery, to reduce packet sizes at the source.

In some cases a provider edge router is able to fragment an IPv4 packet before it enters a pseudowire. If the router can fragment and forward IPv4 packets with the DF bit clear in the same way an IPv4 router does, it may fragment packets arriving from the customer edge and forward the fragments with the framing for that attachment circuit over the pseudowire. Architecturally, the IPv4 fragmentation happens before reaching the pseudowire, presenting multiple frames to the pseudowire to forward in the normal manner for that pseudowire type, so the method is entirely transparent to the pseudowire encapsulation and to the remote end of the pseudowire. The fragments are ultimately reassembled on the destination IPv4 host in the normal way. IPv6 packets are not to be fragmented in this manner.
sections.plainLanguage: Before fragmenting a pseudowire frame, the usual answer is to make the frame smaller in the first place, by setting the right maximum packet sizes along the path. A router may also split an IPv4 packet itself before it enters the tunnel, which the far end notices only as a normal IP packet. IPv6 packets are not split that way.

sections.title: Fragmentation with MPLS
sections.content:
When the signalling procedures of the LDP-based pseudowire setup are in use, there is a Pseudowire Interface Parameter sub-TLV type used to signal the use of fragmentation when advertising a VC label. Its parameter type is 0x09 and its length is 4.

The presence of this parameter in the VC FEC element indicates that the receiver is able to reassemble fragments when the control word is in use for the VC label being advertised. It does not obligate the sender to use fragmentation; it is simply an indication that the sender may use it. The sender must not use fragmentation if the parameter is not present in the VC FEC element. If that signalling is not in use at all, then whether or not to use fragmentation must be configured in the sender.

The MPLS-based pseudowire uses a control word in which the B and E fragmentation bits sit in positions 8 and 9. The two bits together say what a packet holds: 00 means the entire unfragmented payload is carried in a single packet, 01 means the packet carries the first fragment, 10 means the packet carries the last fragment, and 11 means the packet carries an intermediate fragment.

These values are the reverse of the ones used by the PPP Multilink Protocol, which is the fragmentation method this document is based on. In that method the B bit is set on the first fragment, the E bit on the last, and a complete unfragmented frame has both set. PWE3 inverts the values while keeping the operational meaning, so that a complete frame, and an implementation that only supports complete frames, can simply leave both bits at zero.

Path MTU discovery may be used to determine the maximum size for fragments, and the maximum size may also be configured. The signaled Interface MTU parameter should be used to set the maximum size of the reassembly buffer for received packets, to make optimal use of reassembly buffer resources.
sections.plainLanguage: With MPLS, the receiver advertises in the label that it can put fragments back together, and only then may the sender break a frame up. Two bits in the control word say whether a packet is the whole frame, the first piece, the last piece or a piece in the middle. The values are the reverse of the older method this RFC is based on, so that a frame that is not fragmented simply leaves both bits at zero.

sections.title: PW-Specific and IP Fragmentation
sections.content:
When proper MTU management across a network fails, IP packet switched network fragmentation and reassembly may be used to accommodate MTU mismatches between tunnel endpoints. If the overall traffic requiring fragmentation is very light, or there are sufficient optimized mechanisms for IP fragmentation and reassembly available, that may be enough.

When a large number of pseudowire packets require fragmentation, a pseudowire-specific method has properties that potentially allow more resource-friendly implementations. The ability to assign buffer usage on a per-pseudowire basis, and pseudowire sequencing, may be used to gain an advantage over a general mechanism that applies to all IP packets across all pseudowires. PW fragmentation may also be enabled in a selective manner for some or all pseudowires, rather than enabling reassembly for all IP traffic arriving at a node.

Deployments should avoid a situation that uses a combination of IP packet switched network and pseudowire fragmentation and reassembly on the same node, because that clearly defeats the purpose of the mechanism defined here. This matters most for L2TPv3 pseudowires, where fragmentation can take place in three different places, the IP packet switched network, the pseudowire and the encapsulated payload. The MTU and MRU values must be set and advertised properly at each tunnel endpoint to avoid this. When fragmentation is enabled within a given pseudowire, the DF bit must be set on all L2TP over IP packets for that pseudowire.

The receiver's behaviour follows the same pattern as the PPP Multilink Protocol with one difference: reordering fragments before reassembly is optional, and receivers may choose to drop frames when a lost fragment is detected. When the sequence number shows that a fragment has been skipped, the partially reassembled packet may be dropped, or the receiver may wait for the missing fragment to arrive out of order, in which case a reassembly timer must be used so that buffer resources are not held for too long. Dropping out-of-order fragments gives a considerable scalability advantage for equipment doing reassembly, but if the fragments of a frame are consistently received out of order, the frame is never delivered, which can amount to an effective denial of service to a higher-level application. Implementations that fragment a pseudowire frame must therefore at least ensure that all fragments are sent in order from their own egress point. An implementation may also limit how many fragmented frames it reassembles at once, on one pseudowire or across a set of them, so that reassembly resources are shared more evenly.
sections.plainLanguage: If only a little traffic needs splitting, letting the IP layer do it is simpler. If a lot does, splitting at the pseudowire lets a router budget buffers per tunnel. The two should not be used together on the same node, and the receiver may drop a frame whose pieces arrive out of order, which is cheaper but means a badly behaved sender can starve its own frames.

sections.title: Advertising Support with L2TP
sections.content:
Two new attribute value pairs are defined to advertise maximum receive unit values and reassembly support in L2TP. They apply to L2TPv3 and L2TPv2, and may be present in the Incoming-Call-Request, Incoming-Call-Reply, Incoming-Call-Connected, Outgoing-Call-Request, Outgoing-Call-Reply, Outgoing-Call-Connected, or Set-Link-Info messages. The most recent value received always takes precedence over a previous value, and it must be dynamic over the life of the session if it is received via the Set-Link-Info message. One of the two new attributes, MRRU, is used to advertise that PWE3 reassembly is supported by the sender of the attribute, and reassembly support may be unidirectional.

The MRU attribute, number 94, is the maximum size, in octets, of a fragmented or complete pseudowire frame, including L2TP encapsulation, that the advertising side can receive. The advertised value does not include the PSN header, that is the IP and or UDP header. This attribute does not imply that PWE3 fragmentation or reassembly is supported; if reassembly is not enabled or is unavailable, the attribute may be used on its own to advertise the maximum receive unit for a complete frame. The attribute may be hidden, the H bit may be 0 or 1, the mandatory bit should be 0, the length before hiding is 8, and the Vendor ID is the IETF Vendor ID of 0.

The MRRU attribute, number 95, is the maximum size, in octets, of a reassembled frame, including any pseudowire framing but not including the L2TP encapsulation or the L2-specific sublayer. Its presence signifies the ability to receive pseudowire fragments and reassemble them. Packet fragments must not be sent by a peer that has not received this attribute in a control message, and if the MRRU is present in a message, the MRU attribute must be present as well. The MRRU should be used to set the maximum size of the reassembly buffer for received packets, to make optimal use of reassembly buffer resources.

IANA is asked to define the two new attribute values, and to assign two reserved bits in the Default L2-Specific Sublayer and two in the leading bits of the L2TPv2 message header. The Fragmentation Indicator interface parameter had already been allocated, so no further action is needed for it.
sections.plainLanguage: Over L2TP, each side says two things: the biggest frame it can take, and the biggest frame it can put back together. A sender may only send fragments to a peer that has said it can reassemble them, and the two values have to travel together when the reassembly one does.

sections.title: Where the B and E Bits Live
sections.content:
For L2TPv3 encapsulation, the B and E bits are defined as bits 2 and 3 in the leading bits of the Default L2-Specific Sublayer, with the S sequence bit as defined in the L2TPv3 specification. The sublayer looks like this, with the B and E bits marked in the first byte and the sequence number in the remaining three:

|x|S|B|E|x|x|x|x|              Sequence Number                  |

The location of the B and E bits for pseudowire types that use a variant of the L2-specific sublayer is outside the scope of this document. When fragmentation is used, an L2-Specific Sublayer with B and E bits defined must be present in all data packets for a given session, and its presence and format are advertised with the L2-Specific Sublayer AVP, attribute type 69, defined in the L2TPv3 specification.

For L2TPv2 encapsulation, the B and E bits are defined as bits 8 and 9 in the leading bits of the L2TPv2 message header, in the same place as the T, L, S, O and P flags and just before the version field.
sections.plainLanguage: The two bits about fragments sit in different places depending on the tunnel: in the second and third bit of the L2TPv3 sublayer, and in the eighth and ninth bit of the L2TPv2 header. Everything else in those headers stays as it was.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
As with any additional protocol construct, each level of complexity adds the potential to exploit protocol and implementation errors. Implementers should be especially careful not to tie up an abundance of resources, even for the most pathological combination of packet fragments that could be received. Beyond these general implementation quality issues, there are no known notable security issues with the mechanism defined here, and the PPP Multilink Protocol on which this document is based, and its derivatives, have been widely implemented and extensively used.

Two documents describe potential network attacks associated with IP fragmentation and reassembly. They attempt to bypass IP access controls by sending carefully formed tiny fragments, or by exploiting the IP offset field to cause fragments to overlap and rewrite interesting portions of an IP packet after access checks have been performed. The second of these is not an issue with the pseudowire-specific method, because there is no offset field, but implementations must be sure not to allow more than one whole fragment to overwrite another in a reconstructed frame. The first may still be a concern if packet filtering and access controls are placed on tunneled frames within the pseudowire encapsulation. To circumvent any possible attack of either kind, all filtering and access controls should be applied to the resulting reconstructed frame rather than to the pseudowire fragments.
sections.plainLanguage: The main risk is that a sender can tie up a router's memory with a flood of fragments, so implementations have to limit the resources they spend on reassembly. Any filtering should be done on the frame after it has been put back together, not on the individual pieces, because a piece on its own says little about what the whole frame is.

viz.caption: WAYS TO DEAL WITH A FRAME THAT IS TOO BIG

items.title: Manage the MTU
items.text: Set the right maximum sizes between the customer and provider edge routers and across the packet network, and use path MTU discovery to shrink packets at the source.

items.title: Fragment the IPv4 packet
items.text: The provider edge router splits an IPv4 packet with the DF bit clear before it enters the pseudowire, and the destination host reassembles it. IPv6 packets are not split this way.

items.title: Let the IP layer split it
items.text: IP packet switched network fragmentation and reassembly, which is enough when the traffic needing it is light.

items.title: Split the pseudowire frame
items.text: The method in this RFC, which lets buffers be budgeted per pseudowire and can be enabled for selected pseudowires only.

items.label: Unfragmented payload
items.desc: The entire, unfragmented payload is carried in a single packet.

items.label: First fragment
items.desc: The packet carries the first fragment.

items.label: Last fragment
items.desc: The packet carries the last fragment.

items.label: Intermediate fragment
items.desc: The packet carries an intermediate fragment.
